prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Fifteen, Before, For

outputs.L1:
Fifteen years on, the old tollbooth keeper remains at his post, though he can no longer break a twenty—his brains, regrettably, blown out—nor offer the directions I've long since forgotten. I did telephone ahead, believe it or not. Before I can so much as blink, I find myself parked before the impossibly small, unlit house. My finger presses the buried bell—nothing answers. I have walked in circles for hours now, and I hate to be the one to say it, but no one is home in Zanesville, Ohio.

My dusty toothbrush waits for me, of this much I remain certain, as does my teenage reflection in the dust-dimmed mirror. Only now I fear I shall have to disturb the fine, slow snow of dust that has been settling, year upon year, on my blanket and my hair—must don my dust-covered clothes and walk soundlessly, trailing my eternal lunar footprints down the windless hall and, at last, down the stairs.

It won't happen overnight. But one of these days I will arrive; I will descend to sit with the father—the elderly father, strictly speaking, of one who was never truly there. I will sit down and eat my bowl of dust, like all the rest.
outputs.L2:
After a decade and a half, that same tollbooth attendant remains at his station—unable to make change for a twenty (his brains, sadly, have been blown out), and equally incapable of giving directions I've long forgotten. I did call ahead, believe it or not. Yet somehow, before I have time to register it, my car sits idling before this astonishingly tiny, darkened house. My finger presses against the doorbell hidden beneath grime—still, nothing answers. Having wandered these streets for what feels like endless hours, I must confess an unwelcome truth: not a single soul remains in Zanesville, Ohio.

Somewhere, I'm certain, my toothbrush sits gathering dust, and behind that clouded mirror, my adolescent face still lingers, patient and unchanged. What terrifies me now is the prospect of finally breaking that gentle, undisturbed layer of dust—accumulated silently across countless years upon my sheets, my very hair—of pulling on those dust-caked garments and creeping soundlessly forward, leaving behind footprints like something imprinted on the moon's surface, moving through that motionless corridor toward the staircase below.

This won't happen quickly, I know. But eventually—someday—I'll make my way down to join him: my father, sitting there, technically speaking, having never truly existed in any real sense. I'll take my seat beside him and, like everyone else before me, consume my portion of dust.
outputs.L3:
**Return**

Fifteen years had passed since I last came this way, and yet the tollbooth keeper was still there—still at his post, as if time had simply forgotten to move him along with everything else. But something was wrong. His hands rested on the counter at an unnatural angle, and there was blood, unexplained and strangely bloodless in its stillness, pooled like spilled ink across the worn wood. He could not help me. He could not speak. He simply existed there, suspended, a fixture rendered mute by whatever violence had passed through and left him arranged like this—present but emptied, a monument to something that had already happened and would not be explained.

I had called ahead. I remember dialing the number, hearing it ring in that particular hollow way that phones ring in houses with too much empty space. Someone should have been expecting me. But when I arrived, the house sat small and dark against the evening, and no amount of knocking brought anyone to the door. The windows gave back nothing. The porch light was off. I stood there the way one stands before a door that will not open, understanding somehow that the absence was not accidental, that no one had simply stepped out—there was simply no one to answer, and perhaps there hadn't been for a long time.

I began to imagine, then, what lay behind that door: my old room, preserved as though the house had simply stopped breathing the day I left. My toothbrush would still be there, bristles softened with disuse, standing in its cup collecting years of dust. The mirror would hold some residue of my teenage face, layered faintly beneath the tarnish, as though reflections could accumulate like sediment. My old clothes, folded or perhaps left carelessly draped across a chair, untouched by anyone's hands since the last time I wore them. Even my footprints—those temporary marks that should have faded in a day—I imagined pressed permanently into the dust of the floor, waiting the way everything in that house seemed to be waiting.

There was an inevitability to it, a certainty I could feel settling into my chest like sediment of my own. I understood, standing there before the unanswering door, that I would return—not this evening, perhaps, but eventually, inescapably. I would walk through those dust-laden rooms and find my way to whatever chair he used to sit in, this father who was never quite present even when he occupied space in my life. I would sit across from him, or perhaps beside him, in a room grown thick with the years of neglect, and something in that sitting would complete itself, would close some loop that had been open since I was young.

And so the poem arrives at its quiet, terrible acceptance: that this is simply what happens, what must happen, to those of us shaped by such absences. We return. We sit. We eat a bowl of dust—not as punishment, but as ritual, as communion with all the others who have done the same before us, who have swallowed that same fine, grey inheritance and found, in its dryness, something like recognition. There is no resistance left in this final image, only the resigned motion of lifting the bowl, of eating what has been left for us, of joining the quiet company of those who understood, long before we did, that some houses never really let you leave.
outputs.L4:
The road home should have taken four hours. It took fifteen years.

I don't say this as metaphor, though I understand it will be read that way. I mean that I got in the car with every intention of arriving by dinner, and instead the odometer turned over and over, and towns I did not recognize slid past my windows wearing the same gas stations, the same church steeples, as if the whole country had been built from a single template and I was being shown every copy before I was allowed to see the original.

The tollbooths were the first sign that something had shifted beneath the ordinary surface of things. They stood at the usual intervals, their arms raised in perpetual welcome, but no one sat inside them. I slowed at each one, waiting for a hand to emerge, for the small mechanical courtesy of a ticket or a wave, and each time there was only the booth's dim interior, a coffee cup someone had left and forgotten, a newspaper open to a date I didn't recognize because the print had gone soft and gray, as if it had been rained on from the inside.

I drove through all of them free of charge. This should have felt like fortune. It felt like being erased.

When I finally reached the house—and I want to be clear that I did reach it, that this is not a story about failing to arrive—it looked correct in every particular. The same brick, the same crooked mailbox, the same maple that had been too close to the porch since before I was born. But the windows held no light, and when I climbed the steps they gave beneath my feet with a softness that concrete should not have, like walking on the top of a cake that has sat out too long.

I knocked. I want to tell you what happened when I knocked, but the truth is that nothing happened, which is its own kind of event. The knock did not echo. It did not fade. It simply stopped existing the moment my knuckles left the wood, as if the sound had never been generated at all, as if I had performed the gesture of knocking without producing the effect of it, a mime outside a house that no longer required an audience.

I tried the handle. Locked, or perhaps not locked—perhaps handles in this place had simply stopped meaning what handles mean. I put my eye to the window and saw dust. Not dust in the corners, not dust on the furniture, but dust as the entire visible medium, a soft gray atmosphere filling every room like a fog that had given up on rising, that had decided instead to become the room's only furniture, the only inhabitant, the only weather.

I asked the neighbors for directions, though of course I knew the way, though I had walked this street ten thousand times as a child. But the knowing had become unreliable, a memory sitting at the wrong angle in my mind, and I found myself needing to ask a man raking leaves how to get to a house I could see from where I stood. He looked at me the way you look at someone speaking a language you almost understand.

"There's no house there," he said, not unkindly. "There hasn't been a house there in some time."

But I could see it. I could see the brick, the mailbox, the maple.

"That's dust," he said. "That's just what dust looks like, from a distance, if you've been gone long enough."

I have come to understand that I will not get inside today. Perhaps not this year. The tollbooths will continue to wave me through toward a destination that keeps receding at the exact speed of my approach, and the door will continue to absorb my knocking like a mouth that has learned to swallow sound instead of make it, and the neighbors will continue offering directions to a place they insist does not exist while I stand inside its shadow.

But I have also come to understand something else, which is harder to say plainly: that eventually the dust will settle enough, or I will lower myself enough, and I will find myself at last inside that gray room, and my father will be there—not as he was, not restored, but present in the way that dust is present, a kind of settled absence, a shape that time has begun to take instead of a person.

We will not speak. There will be nothing, I think, to say that the years have not already said more thoroughly than either of us could.

He will offer me a bowl. It will be full of dust, the same dust that fills the rooms, the same dust the whole house has been quietly becoming while I drove through empty tollbooths trying to arrive somewhere that had already finished waiting for me.

And I will take it. I will sit across from him in the gray light that isn't really light, and I will eat, because this is what has been prepared, because this is apparently what a homecoming is, after enough years have passed—not the reunion you imagined on the long drive, not the door swinging open, not your name called out in recognition, but this instead: a bowl, a father, a substance made of everything that used to be solid, now fine enough to swallow, now finally, terribly, yours.
outputs.L5:
# Fifteen Before

Fifteen minutes before the meeting, she still hadn't found her notes.

The office buzzed with the usual pre-gathering chaos—papers shuffling, coffee cups clinking, someone laughing too loudly at a joke that wasn't that funny. But for Sarah, time had narrowed to a single, urgent question: where had she put the folder?

She'd had it yesterday. She was sure of that much. Fifteen pages of careful analysis, prepared for exactly this moment, now vanished into the black hole that her desk had become. For years she'd meant to organize her workspace, and for just as many years, she'd failed.

She checked her bag. Nothing. She checked the drawer where important things went to disappear. Nothing there either. The clock on the wall seemed to tick louder with each passing second, as if mocking her for the fifteen minutes that were rapidly shrinking to ten, then five.

For a moment, panic threatened to take over. But then she remembered—she'd left the folder in the break room, right before pouring herself that ill-advised third coffee. She'd set it down "just for a second" while she fixed her mug.

Relief flooded through her as she retrieved it, folder intact, notes exactly where she'd left them. She walked into the meeting with two minutes to spare, breathless but prepared.

Sometimes the things we search for most desperately are hiding in the most obvious places—right where we left them, waiting patiently for us to remember.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about returning to a childhood home in Zanesville, Ohio, where everything is covered in dust and time has stopped.
counterfactuals.output:
The house on Blue Avenue keeps its own weather now, a permanent November inside the walls, and dust falls upward in some rooms if you're not careful about which doorways you trust.

I came back to Zanesville because my mother called, or didn't call—I've stopped being sure which calls were real and which arrived through the crack under the door where light used to live. The pottery city, the Y-Bridge that goes nowhere and everywhere, four directions folding into the same brown river. I crossed it and didn't feel the crossing.

The house recognized me before I recognized it. That's how dust works—it remembers the shape of things even after the things have left. My father's chair still holds his exact absence, upholstered in gray felt made of settled minutes. If I sat down I would become 1987. I did not sit down. I sat down anyway, in the version of me that never learned better.

Every clock in the house points at 4:15 like a held breath. The kitchen table is set for a dinner that finished eating itself decades ago—plates clean, dust thick as frosting, a cake with one slice missing that no one will ever come back to claim. The refrigerator hums the same three notes it hummed when I was nine, a lullaby with no other verses.

Upstairs, my childhood bedroom has grown a second, smaller bedroom inside it, and inside that one, another, each with its own dust-softened bed, each bed slightly warm as if something just left. I lay down in the third one. I fit perfectly. This should have frightened me more than it did.

Through the window: Zanesville, but doubled, the pottery kilns still breathing orange in a sky that never finishes sunset, dust rising from Y-Bridge traffic that hasn't moved since Reagan, headlights frozen mid-blink like eyes that forgot how to close. Somewhere a dog is barking one bark, forever, the same bark, patient as geology.

I found my mother in the basement, dusting a stair that led only to more stairs. She didn't turn around. "You're early," she said, though I was thirty years late, or exactly on time, dust doesn't measure that kind of thing. Her hands moved through decades of grey like water. I asked if she was ready to leave and she said the house wasn't finished remembering us yet, and wouldn't I like to help, and wasn't it nice, wasn't it nice, to be nowhere together, unfinished, held in this soft grey static that used to be Tuesdays, that used to be June, that used to be the small warm weight of being somebody's child in a river town that time forgot to spend.

I picked up a cloth. I understood I might be dusting for a very long time.
Somewhere above us, faintly, a bell that isn't there rang 4:16.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of flash fiction with a dreamlike, unsettling tone about a man who comes back fifteen years later to an empty house that no one truly left.
counterfactuals.output:
# The House That Waited

The key still fit, which was the first wrong thing.

Marcus stood in the doorway breathing dust that smelled like 2009, like his mother's cigarettes and the candle she burned to hide them. The hallway stretched longer than he remembered, or perhaps he had grown smaller in the years between. His shoes left prints in floors that should have been swept clean by a decade and a half of nobody.

"Hello?" The word fell flat, absorbed by walls that seemed to lean inward, listening.

The kitchen clock still ticked. He knew this was wrong—batteries died, springs wound down, entropy was supposed to be reliable even when people weren't—but the second hand swept its patient circle, marking time that shouldn't exist here anymore.

On the counter, a coffee cup held liquid that steamed faintly, though the surface had gone cloudy with age, filmed like a cataract.

He climbed the stairs he'd once counted obsessively—fourteen, always fourteen—and counted seventeen now, or perhaps twelve, the numbers sliding away from him like something glimpsed underwater.

His childhood room. The bed was made. His posters still hung, but the bands had changed their names in the years since, hadn't they? Or had he only imagined that, imagined all fifteen years, imagined the leaving?

In the mirror, his reflection lagged half a second behind his movements, like it was still deciding whether to follow him into this configuration of himself, this older architecture of bone and disappointment.

"Mom?" he tried, though he knew—had always known, some cellar-deep part of him—that she wasn't upstairs. Wasn't anywhere he could name.

The house exhaled around him, walls breathing in the rhythm of something sleeping, something that had been sleeping since before he left and would keep sleeping after he was gone again, if *gone* meant anything here, if *again* did.

He found his old drawings taped to the wall, dated in his child's hand: dates from next week. Next month. A drawing dated for a Tuesday three years in the future, depicting a stick figure man standing in a doorway, done in crayon the exact color of dust.

The front door, when he turned to leave, opened onto his mother's kitchen, cigarette smoke curling, candle burning, her back to him at the stove.

"You're early," she said, without turning. "Or maybe late. It's so hard to tell in here."

The clock ticked its patient circle. The coffee steamed its clouded steam.

Marcus understood, then, that he had never really left—that some part of him had been standing in this doorway for fifteen years, waiting to notice, while another part walked through the world outside, aging, forgetting, becoming someone who could someday hold a key that still, impossibly, fit.

The house settled its walls around him like a held breath finally released.

He hung up his coat.

He'd never really taken it off.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic monologue mixing dark humor and melancholy about the impossibility of truly going home again.
counterfactuals.output:
**On Going Home**

So I went back—
because some idiot part of me still believes
in the myth of the door that opens
the same way twice.

The house was there. Still standing,
like a joke that forgot its own punchline.
New paint. New owners. A trampoline
where my mother's garden used to argue with the frost.
I stood on the sidewalk like a repo man
come to collect a debt no one remembers owing me.

Funny thing about memory—
it renovates everything behind your back.
You leave a kitchen that smelled like Sunday,
come back to find they've gutted it for granite.
Even the ghosts have moved on to nicer real estate.

I knocked, just to see.
A stranger answered wearing my childhood
like a bathrobe two sizes wrong.
"Can I help you?" she asked,
and I wanted to say: *no, but forty years ago you could have.*

Here's the joke, if you want one:
you spend half your life running from home,
and the other half finding out
it packed up and left without you.
The town renamed the street.
The oak tree died of something
oak trees apparently die of.
Even grief needs a zip code, and mine
got reassigned.

I saw an old friend at the gas station.
We talked like two people
reading each other's obituaries aloud, politely,
before the fact. *You look good,* he said—
the eulogy version of *hello.*

There's no home to go home to.
Just a diorama built by nostalgia,
that con artist, that sweet-talking realtor
selling you a house that burned down
the day you first left it.

And still—God help me—
I keep driving past the old address,
like maybe this time the lights will be on,
like maybe this time my mother's voice
will still fit through that window,
like maybe this time
I won't be the stranger
knocking on my own life,
asking to come in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short literary piece in the style of a prose poem that blends absurdist details (a dead tollbooth keeper, a bowl of dust) with themes of memory and homecoming.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Return

The road forgets you before you forget the road. This is the first thing you learn coming back, gravel turning to grief under the tires, the mile markers counting down like a countdown to something that already happened.

At the tollbooth, the keeper has been dead eleven years. Nobody moved him. He sits upright in his little glass house, cap still tilted at the angle of a man expecting change, and the gate arm rises anyway when you approach—some circuit still faithful, still doing its one job long after faith stopped meaning anything to the man who taught it. You wave. He doesn't wave back. This is the most honest exchange you've had in years.

Your mother's kitchen holds a bowl of dust where the fruit used to be. Not dusty fruit—just dust, holding the shape of apples, the ghost-curve of a pear, as if the actual fruit had evaporated slowly enough to leave a memory of its own gravity. You do not touch it. Some inheritances are meant only to be witnessed.

The house remembers you differently than you remember it. The hallway has grown narrower, or you've grown wider with all the years you carried out and never quite put down. The doorframe still holds your childhood heights in pencil, dates beside them like tiny tombstones for the people you used to almost be. Age nine. Age twelve. Age: *stop growing, we can't keep marking you.*

You sit at the table across from the bowl of dust and you understand, finally, that homecoming is just this—the discovery that everything continued without you, patient and strange, the dead keeper still lifting his arm for travelers, the fruit still holding its shape after the substance left, your own name still written on a door in a hand you no longer recognize as yours.

Somewhere outside, the gate arm lowers again, waiting for the next car, the next stranger coming home to a house that kept his height but lost his weight, his name but not his face.

The dust does not stir. The dust has learned, better than you ever will, how to keep a shape after everything real has gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an introspective, stream-of-consciousness narrative about a man haunted by the idea of returning to his estranged father’s house, using dust and silence as recurring symbols.
counterfactuals.output:
The house sits at the end of Maple Hollow Road like a held breath, and I have been driving past it for three weeks now, always at dusk, always slowing but never stopping, my foot hovering over the brake like it's hovering over some decision I haven't made yet, may never make, because what does it mean to go back to a place that stopped being home before I even knew what home was supposed to feel like.

Dust. I keep thinking about the dust. How it must have settled on everything by now—on the piano nobody played after mother left, on the recliner shaped forever like the absence of his body, on the mantle where our photographs used to stand until they didn't, until he turned them face-down or threw them out entirely, I never asked, never wanted to know which was worse. Dust doesn't judge. Dust just accumulates, patient the way grief is patient, the way silence is patient, waiting in corners for someone to finally sit still long enough to notice it's been there all along.

I called him once, four years ago. The silence on the line was its own kind of dust, settling between us with each second neither of us spoke, and I remember thinking: this is what our relationship has become, this hollow static, this held nothing. He said my name like it was a word in a foreign language he'd once known fluently. I said his back the same way. Two men speaking dead languages to each other, both of us too proud or too broken to translate.

The house. God, the house. I picture the dust motes floating in whatever light still manages to breach those curtains, if the curtains are even still there, if anything is still there, or if it's all just been swallowed by that particular quiet that empty houses generate—not the absence of sound but the presence of something else, something that fills the space sound used to occupy. I think grief makes its own weather in empty rooms. I think silence isn't nothing. It's the loudest thing I know.

What would I find. A recliner holding the shape of a body that gave up trying to be a father. Dust thick as felt on the windowsills, and beneath it, maybe, some intention—dust settles slow, gives you time to change your mind, unlike silence, which arrives instantly and never really leaves.

I keep circling this house in my mind the way I circle it in my car, this dusk-time ritual, this refusal to commit to arrival. Maybe I'm afraid the door will open easy, without resistance, and that will somehow be worse than finding it locked. Maybe I'm afraid of what fifteen years of silence look like stacked up in a room, made visible finally as dust, as the residue of everything neither of us said.

Or maybe—and this is the thought I keep swallowing back down like something bitter—maybe I go inside and everything is exactly as I remember, undisturbed, waiting, and the dust hasn't settled at all because someone has been dusting all along, hoping, and that possibility undoes me more than any grave quiet ever could.

The car idles. The house waits, patient as dust, quiet as an old wound healed wrong.

Tomorrow, I tell myself. Tomorrow I'll stop the car instead of just slowing down. Tomorrow I'll walk up that drive and open that door and let the past exhale its stale breath into my lungs, let the silence finally break itself against the sound of my own voice saying his name.

Tomorrow.

The dust will still be there. It always is. It's the one thing time leaves you—that, and the terrible privilege of silence, waiting to be broken by someone brave enough, or desperate enough, to finally speak first.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
